title: behaviour

lessons.title: Change of habit

grammar.title: Present perfect continuous
grammar.shortAr: فعل بدأ في الماضي ويستمر حتى الآن: have/has been + -ing.
points: Use for or since to talk about duration or starting point
Use recently or lately for actions relevant now
Do not use continuous forms with state verbs such as know, love and have
table: I've been studying Mandarin since last year.
They haven't been listening to me.
How long have you been playing the drums?
We've been working together for over twenty years.
She's been waiting for you since 2 p.m.
exceptions: With live, work, teach and study, the perfect simple and continuous are often both possible.

practice.why: The action started in the past and continues now.

practice.why: For refers to a period of time.

lessons.title: People pleaser
goals: Talk about ways of saying no

grammar.title: Relative clauses
grammar.shortAr: جمل الموصول تعطي معلومات جوهرية عن شخص أو شيء: who, which, where, when, whose.
points: Defining relative clauses give essential information
Use who, which, where, when and whose; that can replace who, which or when
Omit who, which or that when the relative clause already has a subject
A relative clause can become verb + -ing or to + infinitive
table: A specialist is someone who knows a lot about a subject.
Do you remember the time when we went on holiday together?
Once there was a girl whose name was Lilibet.
Swimming is something that always makes me feel better.
Rob Jenkins was a teacher (who) I knew at college.
exceptions: Keep the relative pronoun when it is the subject: a teacher who taught me maths.

lessons.title: That's annoying!
goals: Use phrases for things that annoy you
Use continuous forms with always for annoying habits

grammar.title: How to … talk about things that annoy you
grammar.shortAr: للتعبير عن الإزعاج: It gets on my nerves / It bugs me / I can't stand it.
points: Use phrases: I can't stand/bear it, It really annoys me, It gets on my nerves, It bugs me, It drives me crazy
Continue with when + clause, a relative clause or -ing
Use present or past continuous with always, constantly or forever for annoying habits
table: I can't stand it when people drop litter.
It bugs me when people don't answer my messages.
It drives me nuts when that happens.
I can't stand people shortening my name.
exceptions: Phrases like 'It bugs me' and 'It drives me nuts' are informal.

vocab.example: Talk about things that annoy you.

practice.q: It really ___ me when people drop litter.
Don't get me ___ on people who never say thank you.
practice.why: The fixed phrase is 'Don't get me started on'.
Continuous + always describes an annoying habit.
Use the verb 'bother' to say something is not a problem.

lessons.title: Planet Earth II: Jungles
goals: Use unless, even if and in case (of)

grammar.title: Conditional structures: unless, even if, in case (of)
grammar.shortAr: unless = إذا لم، even if = حتى لو، in case = تحسبًا.
points: even if emphasises that something will not change a situation
in case means being prepared for a possible event; in case of + noun is formal
Use present tenses after these expressions for present or future meaning
table: Unless you hurry up, we're going to leave without you.
I can't understand Liz unless she speaks slowly.
Even if the company pays me twice as much, I'm going to leave.
Take your umbrella in case it rains.
I'll make some sandwiches just in case we get hungry.
exceptions: Do not use will after unless or in case: 'unless you tell me', not 'unless you'll tell me'.

vocab.example: Only in the jungle do lizards soar like dragons.
He's a Draco lizard.
He can travel over 30 metres in a single leap.
